[16] On January 27, 2010, claimant and counsel again appeared for the hearing. This time, counsel indicated she was ill and had not been feeling well. She handed in, again for the first time at the hearing, a detailed psychological report about the claimant, now Exhibit C-4. She indicated that she had just got the report. The hearing was commenced, and one particular issue arose about dates, discussed below. Counsel, in an effort to resolve an apparent inconsistency in dates, approached the Panel and showed the Panel her copy of the PIF, on which she had marked some different dates than what appeared. She claimed that she was going to amend the PIF before the hearing, but forgot, due to her illness.

[17] Counsel at that point volunteered that on this case, she had not provided adequate representation for her client, and apologized. The Panel then indicated, and indicates here, that the claimant would not be penalized for any errors made by or incompetence of his counsel. T hus, in arriving at this negative decision, the Panel has been very careful to fairly consider the implications of any alleged counsel error. Unfortunately, even considering all issues relating to counsel, the Panel has found that there is insufficient credible evidence to justify a positive determination.
Credibility

[18] There were a number of inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence, related to principal elements of the claimant's claim, which were not explained satisfactorily by the claimant. In addition, there was one significant implausibility. Cumulatively, these concerns led the Panel to the finding that the claimant's evidence, on the whole, was not credible. Details are as follows.
Inconsistencies

[19] The claimant was asked how many times he had been arrested and detained in Iran. He said twice. The Declaration (Exhibit C-4) he had filled out at the end of his interview process with Immigration when he first made his refugee claim was brought to his attention. It was pointed out to him that in the Declaration, he had only mentioned one detention, and he was asked why. He said that he was told to keep his story short. As well, he said, the proximate cause of his departure from Iran was his second detention, so he only mentioned it, and he intended to tell the whole story later through his lawyer.

[20] The Panel does not accept this explanation, for the following reasons. The Panel has perused the entire Exhibit R/A-2, which contains the entire record of his interviews with Immigration. In Section 4 of IMM 5474, when asked if he had ever been detained or put in jail, he mentioned one incident only. There is a nine page record of an interview with an Immigration Officer, and in it, the claimant only mentioned one detention. Then, the claimant was given a opportunity to write, free-hand, about why he had escaped Iran, and for the third time, he only mentioned one detention. Later, at the PIF stage, two detentions were alleged, for the first time. The Panel finds that the claimant embellished his story by the addition of a second arrest and detention at the PIF stage, and resultantly finds that it did not occur, and from that makes a negative inference as to credibility.

[21] As for the claimant's allegation that he was told to keep his story short, the Panel finds no mention of this request anywhere in Exhibit R/A-2. At this point, the Panel will address the claimant's allegations and counsel's oral submission regarding the interview process and alleged interpretation problems.

[22] The claimant alleged that there were interpretation problem at the interview because the interpreter over the phone was, he believed, an Afghani. Afghanis, he said, do speak Farsi, which he speaks fluently, but there are some differences, he said, in terminology. As a result of these differences, he said, there were interpretation difficulties. It is noted that the claimant only believed, but did not confirm, that the interpreter was an Afghani.

[23] However, a close review of Exhibit R/A-2 indicates as follows. At the beginning of the interview, the record of which was nine (9) pages, the Immigration Officer indicated to the claimant that if at any time he did not understand a question, or a question is unclear, to let the Officer know. The record does not indicate that the claimant ever did that. The claimant indicated that it did occur, and he had to ask for questions to be repeated several times. When asked why, then, this did not appear in the interview notes, he said he didn't know. The Panel finds that this did not occur, since if it did, it would appear on the interview notes.

[24] The Panel also notes the last paragraph of his Declaration (Exhibit R/A-4), written by the claimant at the end of his interview process. He wrote: "I thank the Immigration personnel for their attitude. They encountered me with respect and compassion. They registered what I said in the computer". This indicates that the claimant, at the time, at least, had no complaints at all about the interview process, in fact, the opposite was true.

[25] Further, on the form IMM 5474, part of Exhibit R/A-2, at the end, the claimant signed that what was contained therein was true, and that he had asked for explanation of any point unclear to him. There is also the declaration of the interpreter, over the phone, that the interpreter interpreted the contents of the form to the claimant, and that the claimant had informed the interpreter that he understood it.

subthemes.text:
[26] The claimant said he did complain about the interpreter, and the Immigration Officer repeated questions. The claimant also said that he requested a Kurdish interpreter, but was told none was available. There is no mention of these exchanges in the record, and the Panel has found above that this did not occur, at least in the interview the record of which was nine pages long. It is not necessary to make any further findings on that, though, for the following reasons. If the questions were repeated as the claimant indicated, and there were no further problems, then there is no issue. Also, the claimant indicated at the hearing that he is just as fluent in Farsi as Kurdish, and in fact he requested a Farsi, not Kurdish, interpreter, at his hearing, and the hearing was in fact conducted in Farsi. The Panel also notes that the Declaration was done free-hand by the claimant, with no interpretation at the time, and it was done in Farsi (Persian).

[27] In response to questions by counsel, the claimant indicated that when he signed the forms wherein he indicated that the information he provided was true and was interpreted to him, it was in fact the next day, and it was not interpreted to him. However, he was asked to sign, so he did. The claimant also indicated that he was in a poor mental state when he came to Canada and attended at Immigration for interviews. However, the Panel cannot accept these explanations. The claimant is a university graduate, and thus should have been able to appreciate the advisability of not signing something, in Canada, just because someone asks him to. Also, the Panel finds that Immigration Canada would not request a refugee claimant to sign something that they knew or should have known not to be true, i.e. that the contents of the form were interpreted to the claimant, although he said at the hearing that they were not. There is a presumption that Canadian Immigration officials deal fairly, openly and honestly with refugee claimants, and insufficient evidence has been provided to rebut this assumption.

[28] Thus, in summary, the Panel does not, overall, accept the claimant's explanations of inconsistencies in his evidence to be the result of inadequate interpretation services supplied by Citizenship and Immigration Canada to the claimant.

[29] There are other very significant inconsistencies as well. The claimant was asked the dates of his first detention. He said they were XXXXX, 2005, to XXXXX 2005. When asked if he was sure, he said yes, except the dates may be off by one day only. It was pointed out to him that he gave the following different dates for his first detention, as follows. In his PIF, section 9, he wrote that it was from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, he said it was in a different year entirely, from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. With respect to IMM 5474, the claimant indicated that this was the second detention, and this will be dealt with below.

[30] However, the inconsistency remains between what he said at the hearing and what he had written in the PIF. It was pointed out to the claimant that at the beginning of the hearing, he had sworn to the accuracy of the PIF, and at the hearing he was alleging that it was not correct in this respect. This the claimant blamed on the interpreter at counsel's office. He said this interpreter copied some dates from the interview record with Immigration, and gave examples that the claimant's birthdate was recorded wrong. However, nothing in Exhibit R/A-2 was pointed out wherein the claimant indicated that he had been detained from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005, therefore the Panel cannot accept this explanation that counsel's interpreter incorrectly copied the dates wrong from what is now Exhibit R/A-2.

[31] Then counsel got up and showed the Panel a copy she had of the PIF, which appeared to indicate some changes in pen or pencil to section 9 of the PIF. Counsel indicated that this was evidence that she intended to change section 9 of the PIF before the claimant swore to it at the hearing, but forgot due to her illness. The Panel did not clearly see what counsel had notated by hand in her copy of the PIF, nor was it requested to be entered as an Exhibit, and it was not. She indicated correctly that the revised Narrative indicated that the claimant was arrested on XXXXX, 2005.

[32] The Panel can to a certain extent understand counsel's point. However, the fact that the claimant, apparently incorrectly, blamed this on the interpreter, and also, apparently incorrectly, indicated that the interpreter had taken the wrong information from Exhibit R/A-2, would tend to indicate that the claimant's explanation should not be accepted. When considering all the above, from this inconsistency, only partially explained satisfactorily, the Panel will make a negative inference as to credibility, although the impact of this finding is partially mitigated by counsel's explanation.

[33] Yet another inconsistency arose with respect to the dates of the claimant's alleged second detention. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, the claimant indicated that he was detained from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. This he indicated to be the second alleged detention. However, in his PIF, he indicated that he was released from custody, and escaped from Iran, in XXXXX 2007, and at the hearing the claimant repeated that what he said in the PIF was correct. The claimant was asked to explain the inconsistency. This time he blamed it on the Immigration interpreter mixing up the dates of the Persian and Canadian calendars. The Panel has explained above why it does not accept the claimant's explanations about poor interpretation during the interview process, therefore the Panel does not accept the claimant's explanation and makes a negative inference in regard to credibility from this inconsistency, unsatisfactorily explained.

[34] The claimant was questioned about XXXXX XXXXX, the XXXXX XXXXX he allegedly supported. He was asked where he died, and he replied Teheran, or Iraq. He was asked how XXXXX, a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX would be allowed to live in Iran, and the claimant quickly corrected himself and said he died in London, and that he, the claimant, had made a mistake. This indicates that the claimant has little knowledge of the party he claims to support in Iran. Given the other concerns regarding the claimant's credibility, the Panel makes a further negative inference as to credibility from the claimant's inconsistency, then quick reversal, on this matter.

[35] Incidentally, counsel submitted that the claimant's testimony should be considered keeping in mind that he has memory problems. The Panel asked counsel if there was any clinical evidence of any memory problems. She pointed only to the third full paragraph on p.4 of Exhibit C-4, the Psychiatric Assessment, which the Panel notes does not refer to memory problems. Thus, the Panel cannot ascribe any of the defects in the claimant's testimony to memory problems.

[16] On January 27, 2010, claimant and counsel again appeared for the hearing. This time, counsel indicated she was ill and had not been feeling well. She handed in, again for the first time at the hearing, a detailed psychological report about the claimant, now Exhibit C-4. She indicated that she had just got the report. The hearing was commenced, and one particular issue arose about dates, discussed below. Counsel, in an effort to resolve an apparent inconsistency in dates, approached the Panel and showed the Panel her copy of the PIF, on which she had marked some different dates than what appeared. She claimed that she was going to amend the PIF before the hearing, but forgot, due to her illness.

[17] Counsel at that point volunteered that on this case, she had not provided adequate representation for her client, and apologized. The Panel then indicated, and indicates here, that the claimant would not be penalized for any errors made by or incompetence of his counsel. T hus, in arriving at this negative decision, the Panel has been very careful to fairly consider the implications of any alleged counsel error. Unfortunately, even considering all issues relating to counsel, the Panel has found that there is insufficient credible evidence to justify a positive determination.
Credibility

[18] There were a number of inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence, related to principal elements of the claimant's claim, which were not explained satisfactorily by the claimant. In addition, there was one significant implausibility. Cumulatively, these concerns led the Panel to the finding that the claimant's evidence, on the whole, was not credible. Details are as follows.
Inconsistencies

[19] The claimant was asked how many times he had been arrested and detained in Iran. He said twice. The Declaration (Exhibit C-4) he had filled out at the end of his interview process with Immigration when he first made his refugee claim was brought to his attention. It was pointed out to him that in the Declaration, he had only mentioned one detention, and he was asked why. He said that he was told to keep his story short. As well, he said, the proximate cause of his departure from Iran was his second detention, so he only mentioned it, and he intended to tell the whole story later through his lawyer.

[20] The Panel does not accept this explanation, for the following reasons. The Panel has perused the entire Exhibit R/A-2, which contains the entire record of his interviews with Immigration. In Section 4 of IMM 5474, when asked if he had ever been detained or put in jail, he mentioned one incident only. There is a nine page record of an interview with an Immigration Officer, and in it, the claimant only mentioned one detention. Then, the claimant was given a opportunity to write, free-hand, about why he had escaped Iran, and for the third time, he only mentioned one detention. Later, at the PIF stage, two detentions were alleged, for the first time. The Panel finds that the claimant embellished his story by the addition of a second arrest and detention at the PIF stage, and resultantly finds that it did not occur, and from that makes a negative inference as to credibility.

[21] As for the claimant's allegation that he was told to keep his story short, the Panel finds no mention of this request anywhere in Exhibit R/A-2. At this point, the Panel will address the claimant's allegations and counsel's oral submission regarding the interview process and alleged interpretation problems.

[22] The claimant alleged that there were interpretation problem at the interview because the interpreter over the phone was, he believed, an Afghani. Afghanis, he said, do speak Farsi, which he speaks fluently, but there are some differences, he said, in terminology. As a result of these differences, he said, there were interpretation difficulties. It is noted that the claimant only believed, but did not confirm, that the interpreter was an Afghani.

[23] However, a close review of Exhibit R/A-2 indicates as follows. At the beginning of the interview, the record of which was nine (9) pages, the Immigration Officer indicated to the claimant that if at any time he did not understand a question, or a question is unclear, to let the Officer know. The record does not indicate that the claimant ever did that. The claimant indicated that it did occur, and he had to ask for questions to be repeated several times. When asked why, then, this did not appear in the interview notes, he said he didn't know. The Panel finds that this did not occur, since if it did, it would appear on the interview notes.

[24] The Panel also notes the last paragraph of his Declaration (Exhibit R/A-4), written by the claimant at the end of his interview process. He wrote: "I thank the Immigration personnel for their attitude. They encountered me with respect and compassion. They registered what I said in the computer". This indicates that the claimant, at the time, at least, had no complaints at all about the interview process, in fact, the opposite was true.

[25] Further, on the form IMM 5474, part of Exhibit R/A-2, at the end, the claimant signed that what was contained therein was true, and that he had asked for explanation of any point unclear to him. There is also the declaration of the interpreter, over the phone, that the interpreter interpreted the contents of the form to the claimant, and that the claimant had informed the interpreter that he understood it.

[26] The claimant said he did complain about the interpreter, and the Immigration Officer repeated questions. The claimant also said that he requested a Kurdish interpreter, but was told none was available. There is no mention of these exchanges in the record, and the Panel has found above that this did not occur, at least in the interview the record of which was nine pages long. It is not necessary to make any further findings on that, though, for the following reasons. If the questions were repeated as the claimant indicated, and there were no further problems, then there is no issue. Also, the claimant indicated at the hearing that he is just as fluent in Farsi as Kurdish, and in fact he requested a Farsi, not Kurdish, interpreter, at his hearing, and the hearing was in fact conducted in Farsi. The Panel also notes that the Declaration was done free-hand by the claimant, with no interpretation at the time, and it was done in Farsi (Persian).

[27] In response to questions by counsel, the claimant indicated that when he signed the forms wherein he indicated that the information he provided was true and was interpreted to him, it was in fact the next day, and it was not interpreted to him. However, he was asked to sign, so he did. The claimant also indicated that he was in a poor mental state when he came to Canada and attended at Immigration for interviews. However, the Panel cannot accept these explanations. The claimant is a university graduate, and thus should have been able to appreciate the advisability of not signing something, in Canada, just because someone asks him to. Also, the Panel finds that Immigration Canada would not request a refugee claimant to sign something that they knew or should have known not to be true, i.e. that the contents of the form were interpreted to the claimant, although he said at the hearing that they were not. There is a presumption that Canadian Immigration officials deal fairly, openly and honestly with refugee claimants, and insufficient evidence has been provided to rebut this assumption.

[28] Thus, in summary, the Panel does not, overall, accept the claimant's explanations of inconsistencies in his evidence to be the result of inadequate interpretation services supplied by Citizenship and Immigration Canada to the claimant.

[29] There are other very significant inconsistencies as well. The claimant was asked the dates of his first detention. He said they were XXXXX, 2005, to XXXXX 2005. When asked if he was sure, he said yes, except the dates may be off by one day only. It was pointed out to him that he gave the following different dates for his first detention, as follows. In his PIF, section 9, he wrote that it was from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, he said it was in a different year entirely, from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. With respect to IMM 5474, the claimant indicated that this was the second detention, and this will be dealt with below.

[30] However, the inconsistency remains between what he said at the hearing and what he had written in the PIF. It was pointed out to the claimant that at the beginning of the hearing, he had sworn to the accuracy of the PIF, and at the hearing he was alleging that it was not correct in this respect. This the claimant blamed on the interpreter at counsel's office. He said this interpreter copied some dates from the interview record with Immigration, and gave examples that the claimant's birthdate was recorded wrong. However, nothing in Exhibit R/A-2 was pointed out wherein the claimant indicated that he had been detained from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005, therefore the Panel cannot accept this explanation that counsel's interpreter incorrectly copied the dates wrong from what is now Exhibit R/A-2.

[31] Then counsel got up and showed the Panel a copy she had of the PIF, which appeared to indicate some changes in pen or pencil to section 9 of the PIF. Counsel indicated that this was evidence that she intended to change section 9 of the PIF before the claimant swore to it at the hearing, but forgot due to her illness. The Panel did not clearly see what counsel had notated by hand in her copy of the PIF, nor was it requested to be entered as an Exhibit, and it was not. She indicated correctly that the revised Narrative indicated that the claimant was arrested on XXXXX, 2005.

[32] The Panel can to a certain extent understand counsel's point. However, the fact that the claimant, apparently incorrectly, blamed this on the interpreter, and also, apparently incorrectly, indicated that the interpreter had taken the wrong information from Exhibit R/A-2, would tend to indicate that the claimant's explanation should not be accepted. When considering all the above, from this inconsistency, only partially explained satisfactorily, the Panel will make a negative inference as to credibility, although the impact of this finding is partially mitigated by counsel's explanation.

[33] Yet another inconsistency arose with respect to the dates of the claimant's alleged second detention. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, the claimant indicated that he was detained from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. This he indicated to be the second alleged detention. However, in his PIF, he indicated that he was released from custody, and escaped from Iran, in XXXXX 2007, and at the hearing the claimant repeated that what he said in the PIF was correct. The claimant was asked to explain the inconsistency. This time he blamed it on the Immigration interpreter mixing up the dates of the Persian and Canadian calendars. The Panel has explained above why it does not accept the claimant's explanations about poor interpretation during the interview process, therefore the Panel does not accept the claimant's explanation and makes a negative inference in regard to credibility from this inconsistency, unsatisfactorily explained.

[34] The claimant was questioned about XXXXX XXXXX, the XXXXX XXXXX he allegedly supported. He was asked where he died, and he replied Teheran, or Iraq. He was asked how XXXXX, a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX would be allowed to live in Iran, and the claimant quickly corrected himself and said he died in London, and that he, the claimant, had made a mistake. This indicates that the claimant has little knowledge of the party he claims to support in Iran. Given the other concerns regarding the claimant's credibility, the Panel makes a further negative inference as to credibility from the claimant's inconsistency, then quick reversal, on this matter.

[35] Incidentally, counsel submitted that the claimant's testimony should be considered keeping in mind that he has memory problems. The Panel points out that no memory problems were evident at the hearing, and that the claimant did not cite this as an excuse or explanation for any of the deficiencies in his evidence. The Panel asked counsel if there was any clinical evidence of any memory problems. She pointed only to the third full paragraph on p.4 of Exhibit C-4, the Psychiatric Assessment, which the Panel notes does not refer to memory problems. Thus, the Panel cannot ascribe any of the defects in the claimant's testimony to memory problems.
Implausibility

[36] The Panel has also identified one significant implausibility relating to central elements of the claimant's Narrative. The claimant indicated that the regime, from the time the claimant left Iran in 2007, until XXXXX 2010, has frequently been interrogating his wife to determine the claimant's whereabouts. He wrote in his revised Narrative that she is required to report to the sepah every two months, and indicated at the hearing that she still is interrogated by them. T he claimant testified that the regime still does not know that he is in Canada, because his wife consistently tells the sepah that she does not know where he is. The Panel finds it implausible that the claimant's wife would not have been forced to reveal that the claimant went to Canada, if she had been regularly interrogated by the Iranian regime for over two years as the claimant alleged. It is indicated in Exhibit R/A-1, for example, the latest US DOS report2 (see page 2, for example), that the regime employs torture, and in fact the claimant alleged that the regime tortured him, and also is targeting him to the extent that he feels he has to leave the country. The Panel finds it implausible that the claimant's wife would not have been forced to tell the regime while being periodically interrogated over a period of years that the claimant had left the country, especially if the regime is targeting the claimant to the extent he indicates they are. From this the Panel draws a negative inference as to credibility.

[37] Having regard to the above, the Panel finds the claimant's evidence to be, on the whole, not credible. As a result, the Panel does not find the allegations purported to support a claim for refugee protection to be credible.
CONCLUSION

[38] The Panel has considered all of the evidence and submissions. As a result of the above finding of lack of credibility, the Panel finds that the claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution, or a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture upon a potential return to Iran. The Panel thus finds the claimant to not be a Convention refugee under s. 96 nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA.

[1] The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, is a citizen of Iran. He claims protection under ss. 96 and 97 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
ALLEGATIONS
From original Personal Information Form (PIF) Narrative (Exhibit C-1):

[2] The claimant is a Sunni Kurd, who lived in XXXXX, Kurdistan. His father was detained and tortured, and dismissed by the military. The education system was taken over by hezbollahi. The claimant worked as an office worker for the XXXXX.

[3] The claimant was politically involved and detained on two different occasions. He had to flee Iran, fearing to be re-arrested.
From Declaration (Exhibit R/A-4):

[4] The claimant worked XXXXX XXXXX, and helped the political XXXXX who were against the regime, as much as he could. Most of all, he was with the Hekmat Party. He and others were working in secret. He was arrested on XXXXX, 2007, but escaped on XXXXX, 2007.

[5] His wife has been fired, and she has to live with her parents. Sometimes she stays with her parents. The claimant is upset as a result and has problems with his memory.
From Revised Narrative (Exhibit C-2):

[6] While working at XXXXX XXXXX, the claimant was with a clandestine XXXXX pro-Kurdish XXXXX. One of the XXXXX, XXXXX XXXXX, was in touch with XXXXX XXXXX, XXXXX of Hekmatism, and others of the group outside Iran. XXXXX led the people in the group in how to advocate for Kurd and Sunni rights. At one of the meetings, the group was named XXXXX Liberation Group of Kurdistan, and that appeared on the bottom of each XXXXX. He became seriously active in the group in the XXXXX of 1996. They distributed flyers, held meetings and peaceful rallies, all on a clandestine basis.

[7] On XXXXX, 2005, XXXXX XXXXX, an Iranian Kurd, was murdered by the regime. His group prepared XXXXX, which the claimant printed at his work. XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. There were Kurd protests, the sepah attacked them, and they tried to escape. On XXXXX, 2005, the claimant was arrested. He was tortured for 15 days or longer, then transferred to XXXXX jail, where he was detained for five days and released.

[8] The claimant got medical treatment at home, interrogated at work, but was allowed to return there. He stopped his political activities until XXXXX 2006. After that, in XXXXX 2006, XXXXX contacted him, and he attended a meeting, then a meeting every month. He started being active in XXXXX again. T he last XXXXX he worked on was on XXXXX, 2006. There was a rally on that day at the XXXXX, which the claimant did not attend, but which was broken up by the authorities.

[9] On XXXXX, 2007 the claimant was arrested, detained, interrogated about his XXXXX activities, and seriously tortured. He was released on XXXXX, 2007, and found his wife at his parents'. His parents did not even let him see a doctor. His brother took him to XXXXX village for one night. Then he went to XXXXX and engaged a smuggler. He arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2007. At Immigration, he was interviewed by an Afghani interpreter, who he could not understand.

[10] His wife and family were interrogated. His wife was interrogated, lost her job, and has to report to the sepah every other month. The sepah still looks for him at his parents' house. XXXXX XXXXX has been arrested, and he does not know what happened to XXXXX.
IDENTITY

[11] In Exhibit C-3, the claimant submitted copies of his Iranian Birth Certificate and Drivers License. From these documents, the Panel finds that he is XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Iran.
DETERMINATION

[12] The Panel finds the claimant not to be a Convention refugee under section 96, as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Iran on any of the five Convention grounds. The Panel also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection under section 97 as, on a balance of probabilities, his removal to Iran would not subject him personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. The Panel's reasons are as follows.
ANALYSIS

[13] Credibility was the determinative issue in this claim, that is, whether the claimant provided trustworthy and credible evidence in support of his claim. The Panel carefully considered all the oral and documentary evidence, as well as counsel's oral post-hearing submissions.
The Issue of Counsel Illness and Competence

[14] This counsel is known to the Panel as a capable and conscientious refugee lawyer. However, there were, unfortunately, issues with her performance in this particular refugee claim. Details are as follows.

[15] The hearing was scheduled for November 24, 2009. On that date, counsel and claimant appeared, and counsel proposed to submit as an Exhibit the package now identified as Exhibit C-2. It contained a detailed PIF Narrative, whereas the PIF Narrative previously submitted was very brief. The Panel determined that there was insufficient time to read the revised Narrative in detail to prepare for the hearing, thus it was adjourned to January 27, 2010. The Panel notes and noted that this transmittal was dated many months earlier, March 1, 2009, but was only handed in on the very morning of the hearing in November 2009. Counsel took responsibility for this, citing both illness and simply not getting around to it.

[16] On January 27, 2010, claimant and counsel again appeared for the hearing. This time, counsel indicated she was ill and had not been feeling well. She handed in, again for the first time at the hearing, a detailed psychological report about the claimant, now Exhibit C-4. She indicated that she had just got the report. The Panel also notes that the Declaration was done free-hand by the claimant, with no interpretation at the time, and it was done in Farsi (Persian).

[27] In response to questions by counsel, the claimant indicated that when he signed the forms wherein he indicated that the information he provided was true and was interpreted to him, it was in fact the next day, and it was not interpreted to him. However, he was asked to sign, so he did. The claimant also indicated that he was in a poor mental state when he came to Canada and attended at Immigration for interviews. However, the Panel cannot accept these explanations. The claimant is a university graduate, and thus should have been able to appreciate the advisability of not signing something, in Canada, just because someone asks him to. Also, the Panel finds that Immigration Canada would not request a refugee claimant to sign something that they knew or should have known not to be true, i.e. that the contents of the form were interpreted to the claimant, although he said at the hearing that they were not. There is a presumption that Canadian Immigration officials deal fairly, openly and honestly with refugee claimants, and insufficient evidence has been provided to rebut this assumption.

[28] Thus, in summary, the Panel does not, overall, accept the claimant's explanations of inconsistencies in his evidence to be the result of inadequate interpretation services supplied by Citizenship and Immigration Canada to the claimant.

[29] There are other very significant inconsistencies as well. The claimant was asked the dates of his first detention. He said they were XXXXX, 2005, to XXXXX 2005. When asked if he was sure, he said yes, except the dates may be off by one day only. It was pointed out to him that he gave the following different dates for his first detention, as follows. In his PIF, section 9, he wrote that it was from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, he said it was in a different year entirely, from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. With respect to IMM 5474, the claimant indicated that this was the second detention, and this will be dealt with below.

[30] However, the inconsistency remains between what he said at the hearing and what he had written in the PIF. It was pointed out to the claimant that at the beginning of the hearing, he had sworn to the accuracy of the PIF, and at the hearing he was alleging that it was not correct in this respect. This the claimant blamed on the interpreter at counsel's office. He said this interpreter copied some dates from the interview record with Immigration, and gave examples that the claimant's birthdate was recorded wrong. However, nothing in Exhibit R/A-2 was pointed out wherein the claimant indicated that he had been detained from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005, therefore the Panel cannot accept this explanation that counsel's interpreter incorrectly copied the dates wrong from what is now Exhibit R/A-2.

[31] Then counsel got up and showed the Panel a copy she had of the PIF, which appeared to indicate some changes in pen or pencil to section 9 of the PIF. Counsel indicated that this was evidence that she intended to change section 9 of the PIF before the claimant swore to it at the hearing, but forgot due to her illness. The Panel did not clearly see what counsel had notated by hand in her copy of the PIF, nor was it requested to be entered as an Exhibit, and it was not. She indicated correctly that the revised Narrative indicated that the claimant was arrested on XXXXX, 2005.

[32] The Panel can to a certain extent understand counsel's point. However, the fact that the claimant, apparently incorrectly, blamed this on the interpreter, and also, apparently incorrectly, indicated that the interpreter had taken the wrong information from Exhibit R/A-2, would tend to indicate that the claimant's explanation should not be accepted. When considering all the above, from this inconsistency, only partially explained satisfactorily, the Panel will make a negative inference as to credibility, although the impact of this finding is partially mitigated by counsel's explanation.

[33] Yet another inconsistency arose with respect to the dates of the claimant's alleged second detention. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, the claimant indicated that he was detained from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. This he indicated to be the second alleged detention. However, in his PIF, he indicated that he was released from custody, and escaped from Iran, in XXXXX 2007, and at the hearing the claimant repeated that what he said in the PIF was correct. The claimant was asked to explain the inconsistency. This time he blamed it on the Immigration interpreter mixing up the dates of the Persian and Canadian calendars. The Panel has explained above why it does not accept the claimant's explanations about poor interpretation during the interview process, therefore the Panel does not accept the claimant's explanation and makes a negative inference in regard to credibility from this inconsistency, unsatisfactorily explained.

[34] The claimant was questioned about XXXXX XXXXX, the XXXXX XXXXX he allegedly supported. He was asked where he died, and he replied Teheran, or Iraq. He was asked how XXXXX, a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX would be allowed to live in Iran, and the claimant quickly corrected himself and said he died in London, and that he, the claimant, had made a mistake. This indicates that the claimant has little knowledge of the party he claims to support in Iran. Given the other concerns regarding the claimant's credibility, the Panel makes a further negative inference as to credibility from the claimant's inconsistency, then quick reversal, on this matter.

[35] Incidentally, counsel submitted that the claimant's testimony should be considered keeping in mind that he has memory problems. The Panel points out that no memory problems were evident at the hearing, and that the claimant did not cite this as an excuse or explanation for any of the deficiencies in his evidence. The Panel asked counsel if there was any clinical evidence of any memory problems. She pointed only to the third full paragraph on p.4 of Exhibit C-4, the Psychiatric Assessment, which the Panel notes does not refer to memory problems. Thus, the Panel cannot ascribe any of the defects in the claimant's testimony to memory problems.
Implausibility

[36] The Panel has also identified one significant implausibility relating to central elements of the claimant's Narrative. The claimant indicated that the regime, from the time the claimant left Iran in 2007, until XXXXX 2010, has frequently been interrogating his wife to determine the claimant's whereabouts. He wrote in his revised Narrative that she is required to report to the sepah every two months, and indicated at the hearing that she still is interrogated by them. T he claimant testified that the regime still does not know that he is in Canada, because his wife consistently tells the sepah that she does not know where he is. The Panel finds it implausible that the claimant's wife would not have been forced to reveal that the claimant went to Canada, if she had been regularly interrogated by the Iranian regime for over two years as the claimant alleged. It is indicated in Exhibit R/A-1, for example, the latest US DOS report2 (see page 2, for example), that the regime employs torture, and in fact the claimant alleged that the regime tortured him, and also is targeting him to the extent that he feels he has to leave the country. The Panel finds it implausible that the claimant's wife would not have been forced to tell the regime while being periodically interrogated over a period of years that the claimant had left the country, especially if the regime is targeting the claimant to the extent he indicates they are. From this the Panel draws a negative inference as to credibility.

[37] Having regard to the above, the Panel finds the claimant's evidence to be, on the whole, not credible. As a result, the Panel does not find the allegations purported to support a claim for refugee protection to be credible.
CONCLUSION

[38] The Panel has considered all of the evidence and submissions. As a result of the above finding of lack of credibility, the Panel finds that the claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution, or a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture upon a potential return to Iran. The Panel thus finds the claimant to not be a Convention refugee under s. 96 nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA.

[39] For these reasons, the claim is rejected.
